claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets are primarily governed by variations in the local stacking-fault-energy landscape.
Element-specific chemical short-range order induces variations in local stacking-fault energy.
Alloys with fewer constituents exhibit enhanced chemical short-range order.
Enhanced short-range order in lower-component alloys creates larger local stacking-fault-energy fluctuations.
Larger local stacking-fault-energy fluctuations promote planar slip and twinning.
Chemical disorder in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni homogenizes its stacking-fault-energy distribution.
The more homogeneous stacking-fault-energy distribution of the quinary alloy produces a different balance between dislocation glide and twinning than in lower-component subsets.
Element-specific interactions drive either the formation or frustration of chemical short-range order.
Chemical short-range order modulates effective local stacking-fault energy.
Planar slip and twinning alter yield strength and work-hardening behavior relative to the quinary alloy.
Selected quaternary and ternary alloys will have measurably different yield strength and ductility from identically processed equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Increased chemical order in lower-component alloys will promote twinning or more localized dislocation slip.
The promoted twinning or localized slip may increase work hardening and strength while potentially reducing ductility.
The comparison will vary constituent count while holding thermomechanical processing parameters fixed.
The investigation is limited to single-phase, thermomechanically processed FCC alloys tested at room temperature under inert conditions with negligible oxidation and phase transformation.
